turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: I mean, I think it probably started earlier on with AI Overviews actually, which was the first way we brought generative AI to search. And in that world, we noticed that people were asking these questions and many people were actually trying to put natural language questions into search. And so how can you provide helpful context links to go deeper and make an AI that made sense for Google? That was our first version of these models that could do this for people. And then by building into that and seeing this observation around people wanting more of it, direct access to it, and then being able to ask follow-up questions. You need a new modality. It's going to be really hard to build all of that within the construct of the core search experience. And so that led us to have form a small team of folks, a few people that were technical leaders, a couple designers very small to just prove out what if there was on, almost blank screen, delete, make a little fresh doc with a blinker. (00:44:53): What if there's a new page and you can ask the question, you can ask whatever you want of it. You can tap right into the AI that was originally powering this top of the experience in search. But we invested in making it much more powerful in the ways I described before was in it could search for you. It had reasoning as a part of its model capability, it had multi turn context, so if you had a conversation with it could keep track of that context so it had some unique pieces to it. And what would happen if we tried that quickly. And we basically got, I mean, this was probably five to 10 people worth of people originally.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我认为这可能始于人工智能概述部分——那是我们首次将生成式人工智能引入搜索领域。在那个阶段，我们注意到用户会提出这类问题，而且许多人试图将自然语言问题直接输入搜索引擎。那么如何为用户提供有用的上下文链接，帮助他们深入探索，并开发出适合谷歌的生成式人工智能模型呢？这就是我们最初版本的模型，能够为用户实现这一功能。随后，在观察到用户对此有更高的需求、希望能直接访问这些功能并进行后续提问后，我们意识到在核心搜索体验的框架内很难实现所有这些功能。因此，我们组建了一个小团队，包括几位技术负责人和设计师，仅用极少资源测试了这样一种可能性：如果有一个几乎空白的界面（删除所有内容，创建新文档），用户能否在新页面中提出任意问题，并直接调用最初为搜索体验顶部推荐模块提供支持的AI技术。我们投入大量精力提升其性能：使其具备搜索功能，模型中融入推理机制，支持多轮上下文交互，确保对话过程中能持续追踪用户意图。最初的团队规模仅有5到10人，但我们很快验证了这一思路的可行性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how long ago was this team formed?
turns.zh: 你们这个团队是多久前组建的？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: This was probably over the last year, last summer basically, into the fall.
turns.zh: 大概是在过去一年里吧，去年夏天开始，到秋季结束。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, so about a year ago.
turns.zh: 哇，那就是大约一年前了。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, maybe about a year ago. It was where maybe it started. We were really plugging away on it, and then we saw this little version of it emerge that wasn't very good, but it had this moments of brilliance. It's actually, again, it's kind of like golf where you hit the perfect shot and you're like, "Oh my God." You get that feeling where it's just everything worked. And I asked it a question about, I forget, I was doing something with my daughter and I was planning an experience and it found all this incredibly useful information about park information. It had links to go to the site and confirm a bunch of things. It had Google Maps information that for my daughter, you could walk up, it was walkable. There was early examples like this where it just, it blew me away of what it could find and how helpful it was. (00:46:27): It gave us conviction that we should go and go further. And obviously there's lots of people involved in this type of a decision, tons of support from leaders across the organization. But it just says a little working team that initially, you got to build something and then you have to feel it yourself and it is very entrepreneurial in that way. And then when you see it tangibly, you're like, "What's a version of that? That's good and that could work?" And that gave you hope. And so then we basically built it out and built the first version that launched in Labs basically.
turns.zh:
是啊，也许就是一年前吧。那时候可能才刚开始。我们当时一直在埋头苦干，然后看到一个不太完善的初版，但里面也有一些闪光点。说真的，这就像高尔夫球手打出完美一杆时那种惊喜感——一切都恰到好处。我记得有一次我和女儿一起做活动时，问了一个问题，系统就找到了超多有用的公园信息，还附带链接可以直接确认各种细节。谷歌地图信息显示步行路线清晰，女儿能直接前往。早期版本的这些细节让我惊叹不已，感叹技术的强大与实用性。
（00:46:27）这让我们坚定了继续前进的信念。当然，推动这个决策需要很多人的支持，整个组织的领导层也给予了大力支持。但最初就是一个小团队，先搭建出雏形，再亲自体验其功能，这种创业精神让我着迷。当看到切实成果时，大家会问：“能否改进这个版本？它已经很棒了，但还能更完善？” 这给了我们希望。于是我们继续完善，最终推出了在实验室平台上线的第一版。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the first big milestone was this is working. It was just a qualitative experience of, "Oh wow, this has really, there's magic here."
turns.zh: 第一个重大突破就是功能实现了。那时用户体验简直令人惊叹：“哇，这里真有魔法！”

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yes, it's working. And then we did bring it before labs actually to trusted tester group. There were maybe 500 people externally that we added onto it, and we had pings with them. Some of them were, we actually had friends and family. We tried to treat it a little more like a startup where, because we feel like you got to have people test it to tell you the truth, and tell you when it sucks, because it probably does. (00:47:27): And then they'd message you. So I had a friend who was loving it, but also hating it for lots of good reasons and would just be messaging me all the time, screenshots, "This broke, this broke, this makes no sense." (00:47:37): We had that for a while, and then we got to a point where it was feeling good, the trusted testers were liking it, reporting good stuff, and then we it to this Labs moment where anyone could turn it on and then we used that to make it better with real query data. We could actually see what people were using it for at more scale and so that could tune it to make it better. And then we launched it out to everyone, or at least in the US, and then we've now been on this journey to expand it to all countries and languages and have more people be able to access it.
turns.zh: 是的，它确实好用。后来我们把它带到实验室平台，展示给信任的测试团队。外部测试者约500人，我们不断与他们沟通。有些测试者是家人朋友，我们尽量以创业公司的心态对待——因为你必须让用户试用，听取真实反馈，指出不足之处，毕竟改进总是需要迭代的。（00:47:27）测试者会随时反馈问题，有个朋友对它爱恨交加，总是发消息 complain：“这个崩了，这个没逻辑。” （00:47:37）我们持续优化，最终产品体验良好，测试者反馈积极。借助实验室平台的数据洞察，我们能更清晰地了解用户需求，进而优化产品。最终在美国上线后，我们又踏上了全球化扩展之路，将产品推向全球各国语言用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's incredible that Google went roughly in a year from idea to a significant change to the search experience that's AI powered. I think this is not what people imagine Google is like, and it feels like things are different and things have changed in how you guys operate. What has allowed this to happen so quickly? What's changed? Is it just top-down leadership, we need to get shit done, or is there something more?
turns.zh: 令人难以置信的是，谷歌在大约一年的时间里就从构思到实现了由人工智能驱动的搜索体验的重大变革。我认为这并非人们想象中的谷歌形象，感觉你们的运作方式已经发生了变化和转变。是什么让这一切进展如此迅速？发生了哪些变化？是自上而下的领导力推动，必须快速完成任务，还是另有深层原因？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: No, I mean I think it's interesting how organizations change. I think when you feel like there is a moment in time that is clearly critical to deliver for people, people are trying to get information from Google. We are not able to answer certain things or help people in certain ways and there's this technology that can do it, that creates urgency, and obviously there's lots of people building lots of things and the market's crazy and there's lots of things shipping all the time. (00:48:56): There's a really exciting and healthy moment for us to build and build quickly and I think it's just exciting to be able to capture that opportunity because I think people believe, and I certainly believe that the next year or so of product is going to establish how people use the next wave of products for many years. And so at least I can only speak for myself, I feel this obligation to our users to give them the best version of Google that's powered by AI and that gives them the full knowledge of everything Google knows about the world and information to people and accessible with AI. That's driving a lot of the excitement.
turns.zh: 不，我的意思是组织变革的过程很有趣。当你觉得某个时刻对满足用户需求至关重要时，人们会试图从谷歌获取信息。但我们无法回答某些问题或以特定方式帮助用户，而人工智能技术能解决这些问题，于是形成了紧迫感。显然，市场竞争激烈，产品层出不穷。（00:48:56）：对我们而言，这是一个令人兴奋且富有活力的时刻，我们能够快速创新。我认为抓住这个机遇非常重要，因为我相信未来一年左右的产品将决定人们如何在未来数年使用新一波产品。至少就我个人而言，我感到有责任为用户提供由人工智能驱动的最佳谷歌体验，让他们充分获取谷歌对世界的认知和信息，并通过人工智能实现便捷获取。这正是激发我们热情的核心所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's such a good point that people are building their new habits. It's wild how many people just now rely on ChatGPT and how quickly that happened. And I could see Google being worried that, oh, shit, everyone's changing their habit from searching Google to searching ChatGPT. And the fact that now Gemini is number one. I was actually looking at the list of top, so in the top 15 apps, Google is I think five of them, a third. It's out of control, killing it. When people look at AI Mode versus ChatGPT or Claude or let's even say Perplexity, what's the way you think about the positioning of AI Mode versus these other tools? Is it trying to be a direct competitor or is it just like, "No, it's actually pretty different and here's what it's for?"
turns.zh: 是的，人们养成新习惯这一点非常关键。短短时间内就有如此多人依赖ChatGPT，速度之快令人惊叹。我能理解谷歌会担心，天啊，每个人都在从用谷歌搜索转向用ChatGPT搜索。现在Gemini甚至登顶榜首。事实上，我查看了前15款应用榜单，谷歌占据了其中五席，占比三分之一。真是势不可挡，表现出色。当人们比较AI模式与ChatGPT、Claude，甚至Perplexity时，您如何看待AI模式相较于这些工具的定位？它是试图成为直接竞争对手，还是强调自身差异并明确用途？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, I mean AI Mode's a way to ask search anything you want. It's designed and specially created for information. And so really, it should give incredible helpful responses for the things that people come to Google for. Think about you're planning a trip, you're trying to buy something, you're working through a question for your research project. It needs information and that's really, it's less focused on things like creativity, although there's things that can do that are nice there. It can help you. Just like any kind of core AI product, you can ask it to rewrite something for you, it'll do that. But we are less focused on creativity, productivity, upload a spreadsheet and output graphs for me, we're not focused on that. (00:50:57): We're really focused on what people use Google for, and making an AI for that so that you can come to Google, ask whatever you want and get effortless information about that and context and links to then also verify, dig in and go to the authoritative sources ultimately that people want, and we hear from people. So those ends up becoming the distinct qualities of this product versus more of a chatbot. Maybe you would talk to it like you maybe even have a bit of a, "Hey, how are you doing today," with that chatbot that we have some of that, we see that a little bit, but people are usually coming for information. They're trying to learn something and we focused our product on that.
turns.zh: 是的，我是指AI模式是一种可以让你搜索任何你想搜索内容的方式。它是专为信息检索而设计和打造的。所以说，它应该能为人们在Google上搜索的内容提供极其有用的回复。比如你正在规划一次旅行、试图购买某件商品、为研究项目解决某个疑问。这些都需要信息获取，虽然AI也能处理一些创意类任务，但重点还是在于信息检索。（00:50:57）我们更关注人们使用Google的核心场景，打造专为此场景优化的AI产品，让用户能轻松获取所需信息、相关背景和链接，并最终验证、深挖并找到权威来源——这正是用户的真正需求，也是我们从用户反馈中总结出的产品核心特质。这与普通聊天机器人有所不同。或许你会和聊天机器人寒暄几句，比如“你今天过得怎么样？”，但用户来Google的主要目的是获取信息、学习知识，我们的产品正是围绕这一核心需求打造的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay, AI Mode is not your therapist. Maybe zooming out again a little bit and reflecting on all the amazing products you've worked on, all the places you've worked, if you had to pick two or three just core product principles or philosophies that have helped you build such amazing and successful products, what would those be? What comes to mind?
turns.zh: 明白了。好的，AI模式不是你的心理医生。或许再退一步，回顾一下你参与过的所有出色产品，以及你工作过的各个领域。如果要选出两三个帮助你打造如此成功产品的核心产品理念或哲学，那会是什么？你能想到什么？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: I mean, there's typically three things I think about. If I were to write a book about how to build great products, there'd be three chapters. I mean there'd probably more than that, but three chapters.
turns.zh: 我认为通常有三个要点。如果要写一本关于如何打造优秀产品的书，应该有三个章节。当然可能不止三个，但至少三个章节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I love how short that would be. That's the ideal book.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个主意了。简洁明了才是理想的书籍。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: I've thought about these three areas now for a while and it's like they're always consistently the three things. The first is deeply understand people, and I think we talked about this a little bit with the jobs to be done point and Clayton Christensen's book, which I loved around Competing Against Luck. It really helps you be a student of why someone ends up, in his words, hiring a product. Don't think of users as using your product. Think of users as hiring you to do something for them. (00:52:35): There's this famous quote, I think it's Theodore Levitt had, "People don't want a quarter inch drill, they want a quarter inch hole." So what is someone trying to do? You have to understand that deeply and then you can build an amazing product. And also by the way, when you go back, why someone not using your product? (00:52:57): And so it focuses on these techniques to extract causation. So he actually talks a lot about this interview. He calls it an interrogation where you talk to a user like, "Hey, why do you use my product? Where were you? Were you in bed? Were you at work? What were you doing?" (00:53:11): "Oh, I was talking to my wife in the morning." (00:53:13): "Okay, well, what brought it up?" (00:53:15): "Well, I guess I was reading the newspaper." (00:53:16): "Okay, well why?" (00:53:17): And then you have this aha moment like that when they first decide to use your product, he calls it the big hire. That is information that you obtain ends up becoming the most critical because that is what caused someone to use your product. And if you can study that and understand it, you'll be much more on your way than just building things that sound cool. And so that's the first chapter is deeply understand people. (00:53:37): Second is really around analytical rigor and understanding your problems. You have to understand your problems. And this got is a little bit of what we were talking about about root cause analysis and understanding, okay, the metrics are dropping. Why? If someone's not using your product, why? And really being able to dissect that to get to true root causes. It's like, well, they went all the way to the end and then bailed, and then you understand what turns out that it was most, we actually learned about this and there's a story in Close Friends at Instagram where it just totally failed at first in a bunch just when we shipped it. And it turned out that we looked at the data and people were only adding one close friend to their list because it was mistranslated as best friend in many markets. So people just put one person and then the probability that person saw it and wrote back to you was zero. It's a product which is broken. So it's like you got to understand your problems. (00:54:30): And then the third one's around really designing for clarity instead of cleverness. A lot of people are like, "Oh, we're going to differentiate the design," and we talked about this a little bit with Stories. We're going to make a new version of something, but if something's a standard and people understand it, if you lean into it, you're going to get so much leverage than if you reinvent it, and you have to be really thoughtful around when you reinvent and where you don't. (00:54:54): And I think on this one, there's this great, Don Norman's book. Obviously, Design of Everyday Things is a big one, but he has this incredible chapter in there about doors, and why is it that after all of these years you walk up to a door, and based on how they're designed at times, people still don't know if you should pull or push that door because if you try to build the as beautiful symmetric two handles on each side on a glass door, it doesn't communicate in for any information to you. (00:55:20): And there's lots of, I've seen all the time we've designed new icons when we could have used global icons like, "Oh, wouldn't it be so cool if we used a camera that's kind of a camera but is mostly an AI looking thing and then is mostly, but then has this dots in it that connects it to this other product?" (00:55:37): And you're like, people just, it's a camera. Just put the camera in. Maybe you could add a little thing to it, and that's how you get people to use your products. And if you do those three things, I think you typically can do well. (00:55:49): And then, sorry, the fourth one would be more of the coda is be humble. Constantly and always question yourself. Listen to others, listen to users and be open to being wrong.
turns.zh:
关于这三个方面，我已经思考了一段时间，它们似乎始终如一。首先是深入理解用户需求。我想我们在之前的讨论中提到了"完成任务点"（jobs to be done）以及克莱顿·克里斯滕森（Clayton Christensen）的《与运气竞争》（Competing Against Luck）一书。这本书真正帮助我们理解为什么用户最终会选择你的产品。不要把用户视为使用产品的人，而是要把他们视为雇佣你为他们解决问题的人。

（00:52:35）：我记得西奥多·莱维特（Theodore Levitt）说过一句名言："人们不需要四分之一英寸的钻头，他们需要四分之一英寸的孔。"所以用户真正想做的是什么？你必须深入理解这一点，然后才能打造出色的产品。顺便说一句，当用户不使用你的产品时，你需要反思原因。

（00:52:57）：因此，重点在于通过提问来挖掘因果关系。他在采访中详细讲述了这一方法。他称之为"审讯"——比如，你会问用户："你为什么使用我们的产品？当时你在哪里？是在床上？还是在工作？你在做什么？"

（00:53:11）："哦，我早上和妻子聊天。"

（00:53:13）："好的，那是什么触发了这个行为？"

（00:53:15）："嗯，我当时在看报纸。"

（00:53:16）："好的，为什么呢？"

（00:53:17）：然后当用户首次决定使用你的产品时，你会获得顿悟时刻。他称之为"重大雇佣"。这些获取的信息最终成为最关键的信息，因为它们揭示了用户为何选择你的产品。如果你能深入研究并理解这些原因，你的成功将远不止于构建看似酷炫的产品。

（00:53:37）：第二点是关于分析严谨性和问题理解。你必须透彻理解自身面临的问题。根源分析和数据解读至关重要。例如，当用户不使用产品时，你需要剖析原因。可能是设计缺陷、市场误解或用户使用习惯差异。Instagram的"亲密好友"功能最初上线时就遭遇了失败，因为在许多市场中，"亲密好友"被误译为"好友"，导致用户仅添加了一个亲密好友，回复率却为零。这就是产品设计失败的典型案例。

（00:54:30）：第三点是设计要以清晰为主，而非追求花哨。许多人热衷于"设计差异化"，但我们在Stories功能上已有过教训。若产品已形成标准且用户易于理解，你就应延续而非重新发明。设计时需审慎考虑何时创新、何处创新。

（00:54:54）：在这方面，我推荐唐·诺曼（Don Norman）的著作。《日常物品的设计》（Design of Everyday Things）无疑是经典之作，但其中关于门的设计章节尤为深刻。历经多年，我们依然会被设计不合理的门困扰，人们至今仍分不清是拉还是推门，这正是设计的失败之处。
假如你试图在玻璃门上设计两侧对称美观的把手，这并不会传达任何有用的信息。（00:55:20）我们在设计新图标时，常常会看到这种情况——明明可以使用通用的图标，比如“如果我们用一个看起来像相机、实则以人工智能为核心的设备，再在上面添加连接其他产品的圆点图案，那不是很酷吗？”（00:55:37）而人们往往会觉得，“这就是个相机啊，把相机放进去就行了。”或许你可以给它添加些小功能，这样就能吸引用户使用你的产品了。只要做好这三点，我觉得通常就能取得不错的效果。（00:55:49）然后，抱歉，第四点是保持谦逊。永远要不断自我质疑，倾听他人的意见，倾听用户的声音，并乐于承认自己的错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love these. On that third point, I feel like AI Mode as the name is such a good example of clarity. What is this? This is AI Mode.
turns.zh: 我超爱这些。说到第三点，我觉得“AI模式”这个名字就是清晰明了的典范。这是什么？这就是AI模式。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: We talked about it internally. If you look at it in the tab, it's like everyone know, it's like you see it and you'll know what it is or we could call it something random, but then what is that? And now you're working against yourself.
turns.zh: 我们内部也讨论过这个问题。如果你在标签页里看这个功能，大家一目了然，看到它你就能明白这是干什么的。或者我们可以给它起个随意的名字，但那样又得费力解释了。现在这样反倒自找麻烦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If I were to reflect back these three pieces of basically this is the book you would write to help people build more successful products, it's understand the problem you're solving for people deeply. What's the job they're hiring you to do? I love the, it's lowercase jobs to be done. It's not like the rigorous whole thing that everyone-
turns.zh: 回顾这三个要点——基本上，这本书就是教人们如何打造更成功的产品，关键在于深刻理解用户的问题所在。他们雇你来做什么？我特别喜欢“jobs to be done”这个概念，翻译成“待完成的工作”比较合适。这不像那种复杂的流程框架——

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Exactly. Lowercase for sure.
turns.zh: 没错，绝对要用小写。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. This is just like why are people hiring your product to solve a problem for them? What problem are they solving? So it's like basically figure out what problem they're having then very, through data, understand the problem and whether you are solving it. And then it's just keep it really simple. Clarity over cleverness essentially.
turns.zh: 好的。核心问题就是：用户为什么要用你的产品来解决某个问题？他们在解决什么样的问题？所以关键在于，先搞清楚用户面临的问题，然后通过数据验证解决方案是否有效。接着要保持简单明了。本质上，清晰胜于花哨。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Exactly, yes. And be humble.
turns.zh: 没错，就是要保持谦逊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And be humble. Yes. Okay, important. Is there an example that we haven't talked about that shows this in action of just, cool, here's the problem we found. Here's how we figured out this is the solution and if we're succeeding, and then here's a very simple way of solving it?
turns.zh: 还有，要保持谦逊。好的，这很重要。有没有我们没聊过的案例，能直观展示这一点？比如，发现问题、验证解决方案、判断是否成功，然后用简单易懂的方式解决问题。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: I mean honestly, this Close Friends example, I can give you more from Instagram days was really wild. It took two or three years to get Close Friends to work, and I think people, it totally failed originally. This is the product that lets you add a private list of people and then you can post to your story and then only those people see it. It's like this very exclusive private space so you can feel really comfortable sharing maybe more.
turns.zh: 说实话，这个“亲密好友”功能的例子，我能讲更多早期Instagram的案例，那真是相当疯狂。花了两三年时间才让这个功能正常运作，最初还彻底失败了。这个产品让你能添加私密好友列表，然后你发布动态时只有这些人能看到。这就像一个超级私密的空间，让用户更放心，愿意分享更多内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, green circle.
turns.zh: 哦，绿色圆圈。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Green circles, yes. It's one of the most popular, at least when I was there, was one of the most popular features of Stories and did really well, but it totally failed. And I think what we found out was that you actually used a bunch of these techniques here. So one was we first thought about it as an overall system problem and you could add a Close Friends post for anything. So you could do a feed post or a Stories post, and you also had a close friend's profile. You could see, if Lenny went to Robby's page, we were Close Friends, you would just be like, "Oh, you get to see extra stuff from me on my profile too." (00:58:18): So we shipped it, we thought it would be great. This is the be humble part, wasn't great, had a bunch of, it was just super confusing. You would see this really beautiful photo and then in the feed right after it, this blurry, very vulnerable moment someone's trying to share with their friends, just felt so out of place and weird for the reason people use feed. And then it was just confusing because it had an extra little green thing on it, but it was like that got a green thing and the Stories one didn't. If you open the story, it had a green thing inside the story, and people were just so confused. (00:58:49): And it had this other issue with the list where you're like, "Okay, the list doesn't work because it's mistranslated and people don't get it." I think it was actually called originally favorites, I want to say, and that encouraged people to just do two people on it. But then the way that it worked was, so this gets to the framework, I guess. So deeply understand people. What are people trying to do with this? (00:59:10): What they're trying to do is share a vulnerable thing and be like, "Hey, I'm lonely. Hey, what's going on? Are people up?" And it feels very much like a friend group thing. (00:59:18): And if you only have two people on it, the job that we're doing is actually connecting you to your friends. And if you don't get a DM back, it's broken. And so really what we're doing is getting you a DM and we're getting you connection. We're getting you a sense of being connected to your Close Friends. That is the job. (00:59:33): It's actually everything Clayton Christensen talked about in the book is there are utility jobs and there are emotional jobs. People usually discount the emotional ones a lot. This was really an emotional thing as much as it was utility one, and so product's broken, right? And people don't even know that it's a close friend story, they just see the little head because you have to click on it to see the thing. And so it just, people stopped using it. (00:59:56): We went through and we did these revs where we would simplify it and we would update it and we would go through this change list. Okay, take this out, take this out, change the name, here. And then we saw it was that it was working really well for people who added 20 to 30 people to their list. Because what would happen is you put 30 people on your list and then two of them would write back to you on DM and now you have closed the loop and you feel connected to those people. It's a winning thing. And so we designed the whole system around that, and also only worked in Stories. We were looking at the data, we were trying to understand where it was working and where it was failing, and then we updated the name to Close Friends so it didn't feel like favorites. So it wasn't three people, it's 20. (01:00:34): In the list, we built this list builder where we recommended a set of people based on some cool algo that was created by an engineer. And then we updated the design to put the green ring on the outside of the story so that this was the design for clarity. We were being cute. We thought, I think at the time it was like, "Oh, it's a secret story or something, and if you open it, you see it." (01:00:56): It just was not clear to people. And so we put the green ring on the outside so that users would see it in the tray and be like, "Ooh, what's that little green guy?" (01:01:04): And then they'd click on it and be like, "Oh, this is a private story for me." That system worked and did incredibly well, and that was the process we followed from a total flop to something that was very successful.
turns.zh:
绿色圆圈？没错。这曾是Instagram Stories中最受欢迎的功能之一，至少在我使用期间如此，但最终却彻底失败了。我们发现用户在设计这款功能时用错了方法。最初我们把它当作一个整体系统问题——用户可以为任何内容添加“亲密好友”标签，无论是动态帖子还是Stories内容。用户打开亲密好友的个人主页时，会看到类似这样的提示：“哦，原来你还能在我的主页上看到我的额外动态内容。”（00:58:18）但实际效果却一团糟。用户在动态中看到一张精美的照片，紧接着在信息流中刷到一张模糊的脆弱时刻分享，格格不入，完全违背了用户使用动态的初衷。再加上绿色圆圈的标注让用户困惑不已——有的帖子有绿色圆圈，有的没有。打开Stories时，里面也有绿色圆圈标注，但用户还是一头雾水。

（00:58:49）列表功能也存在问题，最初叫“收藏夹”，鼓励用户添加两个好友，但实际效果却适得其反。我们通过用户研究发现，他们真正需要的是分享脆弱时刻、寻求支持的功能。（00:59:10）但产品设计却偏离了用户需求，用户体验混乱，功能缺失。

（00:59:18）最根本的问题在于，产品未能深刻理解用户行为：用户想分享脆弱时刻，寻求情感共鸣。（00:59:33）克莱顿·克里斯滕森在《创新者的困境》中提到，产品分为实用型和情感型。用户往往低估情感价值，而这款产品本质上是情感型产品。（00:59:56）最终我们通过简化设计、更新名称等改进措施，让产品重获生机。
由一位工程师设计。随后，我们对设计进行了更新，将绿色圆环移至故事界面的外侧，以便更清晰地呈现设计思路。我们当时还想得很俏皮，觉得这像个"秘密故事"之类的，用户打开后就能看到。（01:00:56）但用户还是不太明白。所以我们把绿色圆环放在外侧，这样用户在文件夹中看到它时，会好奇地问："哦，那个小绿家伙是什么？"（01:01:04）然后点击进去，就能发现这是专属于自己的私密故事。这个设计方案效果显著，取得了巨大成功——这就是我们从彻底失败到大获成功的整个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an awesome example. And this took two or three years, you said this process?
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的例子。你说这个过程花了两三年时间？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, it took a while. That was actually one of the longest projects we worked on, but that actually came, the reason we did it was when we asked people to understand people like, "Why aren't you posting to your story? What's preventing you from doing it?" (01:01:32): And everyone had some version of, "Well, my ex is on it. I have a teacher on it. Oh, a friend that kind of is judgy is on it." (01:01:39): It was like this commonality was audience problem. Someone had an issue with people watching them. And so that gave us conviction to go this hard at it for so long because we knew that that was a core problem with the product.
turns.zh: 是的，确实花了不少时间。这实际上是我们做过的最漫长的项目之一，但我们之所以选择做这个，是因为我们曾问用户："为什么不把故事分享出来？是什么在阻止你这么做？"（01:01:32）结果每个人都给出类似的回答，比如"前任在上面关注我""老师在上面关注我""朋友会对我指指点点"（01:01:39）。我们发现一个共同的问题——观众焦虑症。用户担心被别人看到自己的动态。这让我们下定决心长久投入这个项目，因为我们知道这是产品设计的核心难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was this connected to the Finsta, Rinsta trend also?
turns.zh: 这和Finsta、Rinsta潮流有关吗？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: It was actually. I think that informed us. Everyone had a Finsta and there was a Binsta.
turns.zh: 确实有关。我记得这给了我们启发。当时每个人都有Finsta账号，还有Binsta账号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was is a Binsta?
turns.zh: Binsta是什么？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Best friend Insta.
turns.zh: 闺蜜账号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Different, it's this layering of people 20 Finstas down to your partner, Pinsta, and then it's basically like, I made that up. I don't know if it's true, but I'm sure it was out there somewhere. We were like, "Wow. People clearly are trying to hack Instagram basically to create these private smaller group settings, and so we should just make a product."
turns.zh: 这很不同。用户会把20个Finsta账号层层叠加，直到最后只剩下伴侣的Pinsta账号。这就像是人们为了在Instagram上创建私密的小群组而想尽办法破解系统，我们意识到应该直接开发这样的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did you actually do this testing? Was it rolled out to some percentage? Was it rolled out in New Zealand or whatever?
turns.zh: 你们是如何进行测试的？是在部分国家推出的吗？是在新西兰还是其他地方？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, we rolled it out in a few other countries, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，我们在几个国家推出了这个功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay,
turns.zh: 好的，

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Got it. We had a basket of countries that we tried it in and then we would do research. I think it was Australia was one of the first ones for that one.
turns.zh: 明白了。我们在多个国家进行了测试，然后收集反馈。我记得澳大利亚是首批测试的国家之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I was going to ask if you can share the country. So Australia.
turns.zh: 好的，我本想问你能否透露具体国家，但既然你提到澳大利亚，那应该是较早的测试地区。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: I think that was one of the earlier ones, yeah, but every time you ship something there's a slightly different reason why.
turns.zh: 是的，澳大利亚确实是较早的测试地区之一，但每次上线新功能，背后的原因都不尽相同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, interesting. So it's not always Australia gets all the new stuff.
turns.zh: 有意思。所以并非所有新功能都会优先在澳大利亚推出。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: No, although it sometimes is. Australia and Canada get a lot of stuff just because easier for the teams to see feedback from them.
turns.zh: 是的，但有时也会。澳大利亚和加拿大之所以优先获得新功能，是因为团队更容易从这些市场收集反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, speak English.
turns.zh: 好的，说回正题。你对精简团队、打造小型团队、限制资源投入、完全不招人等观点有何看法？你认为需要大量资源才能实现重大突破。能谈谈你的经验吗？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，我赞同你的观点。你需要大量资源才能真正突破瓶颈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, okay, let me go in a different direction and talk about something that you have a hot take on. There's a lot of talk these days about lean teams, small teams, just creating limited resources, not hiring at all. You have an opposite perspective of you actually need a lot of resources to build really big breakthroughs. Talk about your experience there.
turns.zh: 太棒了，好的，我换个话题，谈谈你对精简团队的看法。如今很多人都在讨论精简团队、缩小规模、限制资源投入、不招人等策略。你持相反观点，认为需要大量资源才能实现重大突破。能谈谈你的经验吗？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think there's obviously, depends on what you're trying to build and there's been famously small teams building big impact products, but I think there's this cult of lean, scrappy, fast, throw away your product quickly, keep moving. And I think at some level it's true for internal conviction, but to build a product that works for a lot of people that is based on a technological breakthrough. A lot of times, I see teams just give up to early or under invest in the product, and obviously the space matters. And if you're building a single product that is a way to, I don't know, do something with a digital app that's fairly straightforward, that's going to be different than building a robotics company. So what you're building does change. (01:04:02): But even for software, I mean I think for really hard technical problems, think about the amount of time and effort it took for teams to build a foundational model, and how many years and hundreds and hundreds of people that were needed for that to happen. And you think about these large companies that have had huge impacts on people, and I think particularly for bigger companies internally, something I've seen is it's almost too scrappy because it never gets enough momentum. The product never gets good enough internally and then it just dies on the vine. Whereas if you put more people on it, you have to be careful not to put too many too soon. But I see the opposite more true where people hold on to small teams too long and then you, either takes forever to get to the thing you're looking for. (01:04:46): This Close Friends example I mentioned this actually was a small team. One of the reasons it took us forever was it kept the team so small and scrappy. That loop cycle was so short and by a startup age you'd be dead probably. So you can maybe do that in a bigger company, but as a startup, I don't know if you have that leisure. And so I think you need to actually think what is the group I need to build a version that's great. And from first principles, really think about it instead of just embracing blindly, okay, we're going to be the two of us until this thing has escaped velocity market fit, which it's not always true.
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得这显然取决于你要开发的产品类型。历史上有很多小团队打造出影响深远的产品，但我认为现在存在一种崇尚精益、敏捷、快速、快速迭代产品然后继续前进的文化。从某种程度上说，这种文化在内部信念层面或许有其合理性，但要开发基于技术突破、能服务众多用户的产品，情况就完全不同了。很多时候，我看到团队过早放弃或在产品上投入不足，而行业环境因素同样重要。比如，如果你要开发的是一个相当直接的数字应用产品，那么和创立一家机器人公司相比，所需的资源和时间肯定大不相同。所以开发的产品类型确实会影响策略选择。

（01:04:02）但即便是在软件领域，面对真正复杂的技术挑战时，想想团队花费大量时间和精力才建立起基础模型，需要多少年时间和数百名工程师才能完成这些工作。再看看那些对人类产生重大影响的大型公司，特别是内部团队，我发现很多时候他们过于追求敏捷，反而缺乏足够的动力。产品在内部永远无法达到理想状态，最终只能半途而废。相反，如果投入更多资源，要注意避免过早扩充团队。但我更常见的情况是，团队过于固守小规模模式，导致进展缓慢，最终错失良机。

（01:04:46）我提到的 Close Friends 案例实际上就是一个小团队的例子。我们之所以花费很长时间，部分原因就是团队规模太小、太缺乏资源。迭代周期过短，在创业公司阶段可能就倒闭了。所以大公司或许可以承受这种风险，但作为初创企业，我不确定是否有这样的奢侈。关键在于，你需要评估需要组建怎样的团队才能开发出优质产品。基于第一性原理进行思考，而非盲目跟风。比如，先保持团队小规模，直到产品达到市场临界点——但这种策略并非万能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is definitely counter to the narrative we see on Twitter. Anything you can share about just the heuristic you use to decide here's how long to keep it small? I know there's not going to be this step 1, 2, 3, but just like what I'm hearing is start small to prove out the concept designer PM engineer maybe. When do you find that makes sense to go big?
turns.zh: 这确实与我们在推特上看到的观点相矛盾。能否分享一下您判断何时该保持小团队、何时该扩张的经验？我知道这不可能有固定的步骤，但我听到的常见做法是先小规模验证概念——设计师、产品经理、工程师。您何时认为应该扩大团队规模？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, I think that it's mostly when you've hit the conviction moment. I think there's two big milestones. There's internal conviction. For yourself, do you believe in it? And you believe in it because there's some external validation, your friends, you put 20 friends on it. And by the way, I found out very quickly building startups that if you put 20 friends on something, they're not going to do you that many favors. They're not going to use a product every single day because they're your friend 30 days in, 60 days in, 90 days in. They're not using your product unless you're doing something that's useful to them. And so you get all of this feedback and you're seeing people really enjoy it. You get to that moment. (01:06:17): And then I think that's not a product that would win externally because if you were to ship it, it's broken, doesn't work great. And then you need to, I think invest enough to make the best version of it or as good a version as you can to get it out the door and to ship it. And I think that that, it's like you want to build the right product eventually is the mentality and you can only really do that with the right group.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这主要是在你达成信念时刻的时候。我认为有两个重要的里程碑。首先是内心的信念——你自己是否相信它？而你之所以相信它，是因为有外部的验证，比如你的朋友，你让20个朋友参与其中。顺便说一句，我在创业过程中很快发现，如果你让20个朋友参与某个项目，他们并不会帮你太多忙。他们不会每天使用你的产品，因为他们是你的朋友——无论是30天、60天还是90天之后。他们只有在你开发出对他们有用的产品时才会使用。因此，当你收到所有反馈，看到人们真正喜欢你的产品时，你就到了那个关键时刻。（01:06:17）但我认为这类产品很难在外部获得成功，因为如果你要把它推向市场，它可能存在缺陷，用户体验不佳。这时你就需要投入足够的资源，打造出最佳版本，或者尽可能优秀的版本，才能将产品推向市场。我认为，最终要打造出正确的产品，这才是关键，而这只有在拥有合适团队的情况下才能实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to take us to a recurring segment on the podcast that I call AI Corner.
turns.zh: 接下来，我要带大家进入播客的一个固定环节，我称之为"AI角"。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's some way that you've found use for AI in your work, in your life that is really interesting, really helpful, maybe other people can be inspired by?
turns.zh: 在你的工作或生活中，你有没有发现AI的应用案例特别有趣、特别有用，或许还能给其他人带来启发？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: I think one of the coolest trends ever is how AI is affecting multimodal visual and inspirational needs for people. And we're early in this and I think this is something that I'm actually working on as a project as well, but right now if you think about what AI has done in large part, it was born and grew up in this text modality, it was chat. And so for a long time, if you were to ask it to help you, what's a cool way to redecorate your bookshelf behind you? It's going to describe that to you in text, because that's what it knows. But increasingly, AI is going to be liberated to help in every possible modality. (01:07:29): This is something that we've seen a lot with this explosive use of Google Lens and our image search and image features and with this deep understanding, and what I'm actually starting to use internally and some things that we're excited about more coming up that we actually announced at I/O that we're going to going to be building more of was how AI can help with inspiration, how AI can help with shopping and helping you really get things done that are more in the inspiring bucket of needs versus these core utilities like code, math, homework side of things. turns.zh: 保持好奇心。我差点给公司取名叫‘好奇心’。我觉得好奇心真的很棒。人生中有些事，比如完成任务、理解世界、理解他人、孩子、家人……你总想知道更多，质疑自己之外的事物，而不是自以为无所不知。这很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Final question, okay, so speaking of startups, you started a company called Stamped back in the day, it got acquired by Yahoo. I hear there's a story where you got Justin Bieber on your app and that was a big deal and a big inflection in the success of the app. Can you just tell that story?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。最后一个问题，关于创业公司，你以前创办过Stamped公司，后来被雅虎收购了。听说你曾在app上邀请贾斯汀·比伯，这可是个大新闻，也是该app成功的转折点。能讲讲这个故事吗？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, it's a wild story. Just to scene set a little bit. I was 25 right after Google being an IC PM in New York with some Google friends building this company. So very early on, and maybe in a good way and no idea what I was doing. But basically we decided that the concept of Stamped was to put your stamp on your favorite things, get recommendations from friends and from people that you trust. And so you think of a Twitter feed, but it's all stuff that people think is cool.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真是个离奇的故事。先简单介绍一下背景。我25岁时，正好在纽约担任谷歌的IC产品经理，与几位谷歌同事一起创办了这家公司。当时我们还很青涩，可能方向也有些迷茫，但总之我们决定将Stamped打造成一个平台，让用户为自己喜爱的事物盖章，并从朋友和可信赖的人那里获取推荐。可以想象，这就像推特推送，但内容都是人们认为很酷的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which products.
turns.zh: 哪些产品呢？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: It's like books, restaurants, food. Products, exactly.
turns.zh: 书籍、餐厅、美食之类的。没错，就是这些产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Pillows, possibly.
turns.zh: 或许还有枕头。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Pillows could be on there. I would totally stamp this pillow and then you could discover it. And one of the cold star problems was obviously you want a group of people that are on it that are already using it, that could have some tastemaker type folks. We had a bunch of people that were chefs and we had people who were literary folks. And then we wanted to get a couple people that were more musicians, artists, and these influential folks. (01:19:00): My co-founder and I just basically got the contact of Scooter Braun, who's Justin's manager, and we just sent out an email and we were like, "Hey, we're in New York. We're going to be in LA tomorrow." I think we said something, I don't remember all the details, but it was something like tomorrow.
turns.zh: 枕头也能上架。我肯定会给这个枕头盖章，然后让其他人发现它。当时面临的一个难题是，显然需要一群已经在使用平台、且有影响力的人加入。比如我们邀请了许多厨师和文学人士，还想拉来几位音乐家、艺术家和其他有影响力的人物。（01:19:00）：我和联合创始人联系了贾斯汀的经纪人斯库特·布劳恩，发邮件给他，说：“嘿，我们在纽约，明天要去洛杉矶。”我记得我们大概说了句“明天”，但具体细节记不清了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you were not going to be in LA tomorrow.
turns.zh: 但你们明天根本没去洛杉矶啊。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: No, no.
turns.zh: 对啊，没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: "Do you happen to be there?" (01:19:19): And he just wrote back some one line thing like, "Meet me at this hotel for breakfast at something." (01:19:25): And we're like, "Oh, okay." (01:19:28): We literally went immediately to the airport. I just remember just basically going straight to the airport, flying to LA meeting with him. We gave him the whole pitch, we showed him the product, and then he was like, "Okay, I think this would be super cool. We can be involved and maybe you can help be an advisor." (01:19:44): And we ended up going back and meeting with Justin and showing him the product and even filming some little clips with him. It was actually really funny and it was a really fun moment. And obviously he was using it to stamp his favorite stuff. And so people would go, "Oh, Justin's into this song, or he is into this stuff," and would post that. (01:20:02): It was one of the ways that we got lots of people to try out and see what we were doing. That's a little extra scrappy moment in time, but I think it embodies a good lesson. Just do it now, be scrappy, be immediate. Intense urgency usually wins over thinking about it for a long time, and that's certainly proved to be true on that one.
turns.zh: “你刚好在那儿吗？”（01:19:19）：他回复了一句简短的消息：“去这家酒店吃早餐吧。”（01:19:25）：我们回复：“好的，行。”（01:19:28）：我们直接冲向机场。我只记得我们一路直奔机场，飞到洛杉矶和他见面。我们向他展示了整个产品构想，还让他试用了产品。结果他说：“好的，我觉得这会很酷。我们可以参与进来，也许你能当顾问。”（01:19:44）：最后我们回去找贾斯汀，向他展示产品，甚至还和他一起拍摄了一些小片段。那真是非常有趣的时刻。显然，他也在用这个平台盖章自己喜欢的物品。人们会说：“哦，贾斯汀喜欢这首歌，或者他对这个感兴趣”，然后把这些内容分享出来。（01:20:02）：这就是我们吸引大量用户尝试产品、了解我们理念的关键时刻。这是个充满拼劲的时刻，但我认为它蕴含着一个深刻的启示：立即行动，保持灵活，迅速决策。强烈的紧迫感往往比深思熟虑更有成效，这一点在这次经历中得到了验证。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible story, thank you for sharing that. So many lessons to take away. Two final questions, where can folks find online if they want to reach out, maybe learn more about what you're doing and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 真是不可思议的故事，感谢分享。收获了许多启示。最后两个问题：如果大家想联系你，或者了解更多信息，可以在哪里找到相关信息？

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Yeah, I think on X @rmstein is probably the best single place. And then to be helpful, send me feedback. DM me, just mention me, ping me, let me know problems with Google products, with AI in general, but also just anything. As I said before, you have to always listen to people understand their experiences, so ping the ideas and feedback. That's the best way to be helpful.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得X @rmstein可能是最佳的反馈平台。为了能更好地帮助大家，请随时向我反馈问题。可以直接私信我、@我、提及我，或者告知我谷歌产品、人工智能方面的问题，以及任何其他方面的不足。正如我之前所说，我们必须时刻倾听用户的需求，理解他们的真实体验，所以欢迎随时提出想法和反馈。这才是最有效的帮助方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. What an onslaught you're about to receive of feedback on the search experience.
turns.zh: 哇，关于搜索体验的反馈肯定会如潮水般涌来。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: No problem. Yes, please do.
turns.zh: 没问题。好的，麻烦了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "Robby, why is this link second? Why is my site not at the top?" I can only imagine the kind of stuff people complain about. Robby, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: “罗比，为什么这个链接排在第二位？为什么我的网站不在首页？”我简直能想象人们会抱怨些什么。罗比，非常感谢你能来。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Thank you, it was great.
turns.zh: 谢谢，交流很愉快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was great. Bye, everyone.
turns.zh: 真的很棒。大家再见。

turns.speaker: Robby Stein
turns.en: Take care.
turns.zh: 保重。
